adversarial_test_results.prompt:
By the autumn of 1929 the optimism that had carried the American economy through the previous decade had begun to fray. Factories that had run three shifts a year earlier cut back to one, and the men who had built automobiles and radios found themselves standing in breadlines before dawn. In the coal towns of West Virginia the company stores extended credit for a few weeks and then stopped, and families who had lived on the same hillside for three generations packed what they could carry into borrowed trucks.

The new president understood that the crisis was as much psychological as material. In his first inaugural address he told the country that the only thing to fear was fear itself, and the line was repeated so often in the following weeks that it became a kind of shorthand for the mood of the era. Commentators who had spent years mocking activist government now wrote approvingly of bold experimentation, and editorial pages that had denounced deficit spending discovered the virtues of public works.

Congress moved quickly. The Emergency Banking Act closed the banks for four days and reopened only those the Treasury judged sound, and deposits returned within a month. Farmers received the Agricultural Adjustment Act, which paid them to leave land fallow, and homeowners received refinancing through a new corporation that bought mortgages at face value. Each measure was argued over, amended, and signed in a rush of activity that left even its supporters breathless.

Not everyone was pleased. Business leaders who had welcomed the first emergency measures complained that the codes and boards multiplied faster than anyone could track, and small manufacturers resented rules written by competitors they had spent their lives trying to undersell. Southern congressmen worried that minimum wages would upend the racial order of their districts, and labor organizers worried that the same codes would freeze out the unions that had fought for those wages in the first place.

Still, the sense of motion was unmistakable. In the spring of 1933 the federal government had seemed paralyzed; a year later it was issuing regulations on everything from chicken slaughtering to the length of a shirt collar. It was during this burst of rulemaking that the National Recovery Administration (NRA) was established to administer the industrial codes, with General Hugh Johnson at its head and a blue eagle in the window of every shop that agreed to comply.

The blue eagle did not last. By 1935 the Supreme Court had struck down the codes, and the agencies that administered them were dismantled almost as quickly as they had been built. But the habit of federal intervention survived the institutions that had introduced it, and the men and women who had staffed those early agencies went on to write the legislation of the next decade. When historians look back at the period, they tend to remember the experiments that failed as fondly as the ones that worked, because both were evidence of a government that had stopped waiting for the crisis to solve itself.
